children: The Indian rupee reversed an early fall past 96 per dollar to trade modestly higher on Thursday as likely central bank intervention and traders trimming bearish bets helped counter multiple headwinds.
A U.S. Federal Reserve rate hike and signals of further tightening weighed on the rupee, adding to pressure from high oil prices amid the Iran war.
But dollar sales from state-run banks, most likely on behalf of the Reserve Bank of India, pushed back the tide and helped the currency nudge higher.
Traders trimming bearish rupee bets added to the gains, lifting the currency to 95.90 per dollar from a low of 96.0925 and 0.1% above Wednesday's close.
India's benchmark 10-year bond yield edged higher after the Fed rate hike, while traders added to bets on RBI hikes over the next year.
Swap markets have priced in about 90 bps of rate increases over that time frame, reflecting expectations that India may need to join the global rate hike cycle it has sat out so far.
Peers like Indonesia, South Korea and Philippines have raised rates over the last few months, going large global monetary authorities like the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan.
"Higher US yields and a higher-for-longer Fed policy rate backdrop could weigh on Asian currencies," MUFG said in a note. Regional currencies were mostly weaker by 0.1% to 0.4% on Thursday.

Meanwhile, investors will also keep an eye on developments spurred by the passage of U.S legislation that authorizes the U.S. President to impose stiff tariffs of up to 100% on China and India, among others, to reduce their dependence ​on Russian energy.
India, for its part, has vowed to protect energy security and warned that such tariffs could impact ties between Washington and New Delhi.
